synopsis: Shadow mode runs candidate braking software live on working machines with brake commands disconnected, recording hypothetical interventions; replay and shadow mode are the cheapest large-volume validation methods, and the company already has a suitable fleet [f13467, f332, f333]. The booklet recommends starting warning-fleet logging immediately during October 2026–mid-2027 to obtain field-representative false-positive evidence before the prototype arrives, then using the four-month physical campaign to confirm predictions rather than tune the system [f1600, f1604, f1611]. Nuisance-rate evidence must use representative real operating hours, with warnings, sensor data and context logged and results broken down by site type and weather; simultaneous old/new recording supports paired comparisons, ideally against independent common ground truth [f6912, f1601, f5480, f5495]. Before enabling braking, hypothetical interventions should be reviewed with operators and safety engineers, and frequent operationally unacceptable events should trigger stopping or escalation; acceptance thresholds must come from the organization's own shadow data and vendors' documented switch-off conditions [f10729, f10951, f10952, f11281]. Shadow mode remains open-loop and cannot establish actual braking consequences, including loaded wet-decline stability, following-truck collisions, load shifts, operator resistance or actuator faults [f335, f336, f13471]. No publicly documented heavy-off-road shadow-mode validation programme or warning-data-to-braking certification case was found, and sensor-specific evidence makes the sensor decision a gate for much pre-prototype work [f588, f1253, f2006].
